December 19
Advent 4C — The Fourth Sunday in Advent
Colors: violet, blue
Mic 5:2-5a
Psalm 80:1-7
Heb 10:1-10
Lk 1:39-56
Grace and peace from God our Father and our Lord Jesus Christ, whose kingdom and power and glory we live for and in.

For the last three Sundays of Advent, I have been talking about ways to get ready for the coming kingdom of God. They have not sounded particularly Christmas-y. Well, in part, that's because it's not Christmas yet, and Advent is supposed to be about getting ready for Christmas - and I don't mean baking cookies (don't let me discourage you from baking cookies as they are of particular importance to me) and shopping. I am talking about getting ready for the coming of the Kingdom of God. Or, as Jesus taught us to pray, "thy kingdom come."

One of the problems of the age following the Ascension of Jesus is that we live in an age of expectation. We expect the Kingdom of God to come in all of its fullness *any day now* (and get rid of all the things we hate). Oddly, this is the same situation the people of Jesus' time thought: Any day now, the Kingdom of God is going to come in all of its glory (and throw out the Romans).

When the Angel Gabriel comes to Mary, saying, "And behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High. And the Lord God will give to him the throne of his father David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom, there will be no end" (Luke 1:31-33); I find it had to imagine Mary was thinking of the spiritual sort of kingdom Jesus would eventually talk about.

Of course, imagining what someone else might think about events when you can't ask them is fairly presumptuous. Be that as it may, however, what Mary thought about the events promised by Gabriel didn't matter. Her response to Gabriel was, "Behold, I am the servant of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word" (Luke 1:38). In her response, we find the response of a true servant of God - very much in keeping with how Jesus taught us to pray: "Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven." Parenthetically, regardless of what that will turn out to be.

Though not usually viewed this way, Gabriel grants Mary a sign: "And behold, your relative Elizabeth in her old age has also conceived a son, and this is the sixth month with her who was called barren" (Luke 1:36). And so, Mary rushes off to visit Elizabeth who was then 6 months along.

When Mary greets Elizabeth, we are told that baby John the Baptist, still three months from being born, leapt in Elizabeth's womb. Of course, the only leaping in the womb I have ever experienced is through the reports of others, which is usually along the lines, "WHOA!".  If that was Elizabeth's initial response, it remains unrecorded. But what is recorded is, "Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit, and she exclaimed with a loud cry, “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb! And why is this granted to me that the mother of my Lord should come to me?" (Luke 1:41-43).

One of the fun things about these verses is this is where Elizabeth, who we've named this church for, becomes the first person to acknowledge that Jesus is Lord. Just in case you missed it, Elizabeth says, "... why is it granted to me that the mother of *my lord* should come to me?"

Mary's response to all this is what we have come to know as The Magnificat. The Magnificat is one of the earliest hymns in the history of The Church and we continue to use it up to this day. It begins with, "My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit rejoices in God my Savior" (Luke 1:46-47). These opening lines take us back again to the Lord's Prayer, where Jesus tells us to pray, "Hallowed be thy name." Mary does just that; she declares the holiness of God's name, saying, "My soul magnifies the Lord," and goes on to unpack what she means.

At this point, while I was working on this, I asked myself if there was a parallel here to everything in the Lord's Prayer. My first reaction was, "Oh, that would be a stretch! Just get on with it". And then I thought I had best have a look. As it turns out, it's not that much of a stretch.

Random thoughts can be a dangerous thing. I began to wonder how the Lord's Prayer might be an outline for the entire ministry of Jesus. Of course it is! Not only that, the Lord's Prayer turns out to be a great outline for the Christian Life well lived. All of this while NOT working on this essay (Oh, the tangled webs we weave).

But back to the Magnificat. I will give you one more parallel with the Lord's Prayer: Mary proclaims, "He has shown strength with his arm; he has scattered the proud in the thoughts of their hearts; he has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted those of humble estate" (Luke 1:51-52). Do you see how this is reflective of the part of the Lord's Prayer that goes, "For thine is the kingdom and the power and glory..."? That the Magnificat is all about the kingdom and the power and the glory of the Lord is what makes it the wonderful thing that it is.

The Magnificat being a deliciously packed prophecy of Jesus’ ministry to come seems almost secondary. But then, what is the ministry of Jesus about if not the kingdom and the power and glory of the Lord?

With that, I will leave you with this thought to carry you forward. The Magnificat (and the Lord's Prayer) are also deliciously packed prophecies about you. Yep, you. Well, you and the Christian Life well lived. The lives we are destined to live are lives destined to hallow God's name, for your souls to magnify the Lord's name, living in and for the kingdom and the power and glory of Our Father. And with that, I'll leave you to it.

The peace of God, which passes all understanding, keep your hearts and minds in the knowledge and love of God, and of his Son Jesus Christ our Lord; and the blessing of God Almighty, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, be among you, and remain with you always.
